about: What the players of the winds do, the woodwinds' and the brass's, on the objects' tree (registry/README.md): a node's values are its players'; one a node does not give, its parent's.

resonances.note: usually three resonances of the tract from 0.1 to 3 kHz, typically at 0.3, 1.3 and 2.3 kHz, varying among players and playing conditions

frequency.note: its first peak present for every player, hardly varied with how they played: 200-300 Hz (220-280 in Table I)

peak.note: 1.8-5.6 MPa s/m^3 for most players (to 18 in Table I), a tenth of the bore's

held.note: under notes of about 450 Hz the resonance in the mouth held at a constant frequency, near 600 Hz for these players; over them, it follows the note (offset)

offset.note: the resonance in the mouth about 150 Hz (100-200) above the sounding pitch, on average, in normal playing from notes of about 450 Hz to at least 1400

peak.note: about 9 MPa s/m^3 on average in normal playing, against the operating bore peak's 40-90: little effect on the sounding frequency

glottis.note: the glottis's opening a player's tract may take, from an expert's slit, 15 mm^2 (10 by 1.5 mm, IV.B), to an amateur's, 90 mm^2 (IV.F), as Fritz & Wolfe take them from Mukai 1992's laryngoscopy; a shape's glottis held within it (public/shared/performers/vocal-tract-played.js holdsShape; native/openwind-tuner src/tract_shape.rs Space::baked, which reads it here)

peak.note: pitch bending and glissandi in the second register and above: as high as 60 MPa s/m^3, comparable with the bore's; 32 at 705 Hz bent a note 190 cents

contact.note: the tongue's contact with the reed between portato notes, clarinettists playing eighths at 60 and 120 bpm, piano and forte: invariant with tempo and dynamic (37 ms, sd 14)
[the notes' inter-onset interval, the tongue's contact with the reed]: clarinettists' staccato eighths at 120 and 60 bpm, the note stopped by the tongue (their technique I); sd 31 and 27 ms

silence.note: [the notes' inter-onset interval, the silence between notes]: the same staccato eighths at 120 and 60 bpm, stopped by the tongue (technique I); sd 37 and 43 ms

area.note: the reed's equivalent area under the lip: the slope of the line on the (lip force, mouth pressure) plane above which the reed is held shut, about 3 cm^2, the lip's force and the mouth's pressure over it closing the reed's tip alike (its opening at rest h0 = h00 - F0/(Ka Ar): Gaillard, Koehl & Gazengel 2024, eq. 4, after Gazengel et al.); measured on a Yamaha YCL250 clarinet, a Legere reed of hardness 2, the lip at its middle position

fit.method: claude-scratch/lip-force/lip_notes.py: the reed's harmonic balance (render/synthesis/tools/reed_balance.py) on the clarinet's impedance, its lip eased and pressed from each note's own at mf, its breath held as its share of the closing pressure
fit.data: almeida-george-smith-wolfe-2013, Figs. 3 and 4: a clarinet on an artificial mouth, its written G4 some 50 to 60 c lower as its artificial lip's force eases from about 2 N to 0.3 N, some 5 to 10 c higher pressed to 2.8 N

lengthening.note: how much longer the reed's vibrating length grows a newton as the lip eases from the note's own, the reed lifting off the lay (its pulsation as the square of the length's inverse, its moving mass and area as the length: a cantilever's), none as it presses harder, the reed on the lay to the lip already; so fitted, the clarinet's G4 50 c lower at 1.7 N eased, the chalumeau's notes 48 to 64 c, the clarion's 20 to 42, and 4 to 16 c higher at 0.8 N pressed

turbulence.reason: ours, to be fitted: the flow through the reed's channel turbulent, its fluctuation a share of the flow per root hertz, white to the engine's own rate (native/openwind src/stream.rs turbulence, the slit's coefficient moved by it each step, and the offline renders' openwind_compiled.py alike; public/shared/performers/turbulence.js turbulenceOf); none until fitted to players' held notes, the noise between their harmonics on the anechoic recordings (Weinzierl et al. 2017; research/MODELING_GAPS.md, "No turbulent noise in the reed's or the lips' flow")

searched.query: turbulent noise in a clarinet's reed channel's flow, its level measured
searched.found: none measured: J. O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Single-Reed Theory' -- synthesis models' noise modulated by the reed 'despite a lack of firm basis in acoustic measurements to date', turbulence near the reed's closing the basic model's chief omission; a reed channel's flow laminar-like below a Reynolds number of about 4000, seldom reached in saxophones and clarinets (TU Delft repository); a synthesis patent's noise following the breath, its level unmeasured

leap.reason: ours: the time a leap within one register takes its fingers, an octave of it; to be measured on the engine, a slur from note to note held shorter until its second note no longer speaks (research/IDIOM_AS_RELATIONS.md)

resonances.note: a modest first peak consistently around 150-250 Hz, and the next, of primary interest, typically around 1 kHz; measured on the tenor, five expert and three amateur saxophonists

frequency.note: a modest peak in the mouth consistently observed around 150-250 Hz, not tuned in any playing condition studied (III.C: 253 and 242 Hz under a standard and an altissimo note)

peak.note: not more than several MPa s/m^3: 2.5 (240 Hz, a soft note), 3.3 and 2.9 (253 and 242 Hz), 8 under one multiphonic's tract

held.note: over the standard range the second resonance from about 500 to 1100 Hz with no simple relation to the note, experts' broadly spread, amateurs' in two bands at about 650 and 1100 Hz; the lower band where it is held

offset.note: in the altissimo (on the tenor from sounding 659-698 Hz) experts tune a strong resonance near the note, typically not more than 100 Hz apart, on or above it rather than below: the note 921 Hz, 60 Hz below its peak at 980; toward the upper standard range experts already adjust it

peak.note: over the standard range amateurs' 0.4-6 MPa s/m^3, experts' rising from about 1 to about 10 near the top of the second register; 3 in normal playing at C#5 against the bore's operating 62

to play the weaker bore resonances (typically below 30 MPa s/m^3) experienced saxophonists make a strong resonance with impedance maxima ranging from 10 to 40 MPa s/m^3, comparable with the bore's: 33 at 980 Hz against the bore's 9.8 at 949; amateurs, who did not, could not play the altissimo (Chen, Smith & Wolfe 2008)

bugling, 22-28 MPa s/m^3 near the 7th to 12th bore peaks; a pitch bend raising the mouth's peak almost sixfold from 3, the note 91 Hz (300 cents) below its fingering's; 10-40 in bugling and the altissimo

searched.found: none measured: C. Vergez & X. Rodet's trumpet model (ICMC 2001), the jet out of the lips losing its energy to turbulence in the mouthpiece's cup, no noise level; Adachi & Sato's lips, and Giordano's (ISMA 2017) Navier-Stokes flow over them, no level given
